textTitles: What happens to a satellite when it dies
The colour that built an industry
Is it worth restoring a building?

texts.title: What happens to a satellite when it dies

paragraphs.text: Everything that has been put into orbit is still there unless somebody arranged for it not to be. A satellite that stops working does not fall; it continues on the path it had, at a speed of several kilometres a second, and becomes an obstacle rather than an asset. The number of such objects large enough to be tracked is in the tens of thousands, and the number too small to track and large enough to destroy a spacecraft is in the millions. A fleck of paint at those speeds carries the energy of a rifle bullet.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The behaviour of the debris depends almost entirely on how high it is. Below about six hundred kilometres the atmosphere, thin as it is, still drags on an object enough to bring it down within a few years, and a satellite that ends its life there disposes of itself. Above a thousand kilometres there is effectively no drag, and an object left in that band will still be there in a thousand years. The difference between the two regimes is a few hundred kilometres and the whole of the problem.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Collisions produce far more debris than launches do. Two events, a satellite that was destroyed deliberately in a test and a collision between an active and a defunct satellite, together created several thousand trackable fragments and a much larger number of untrackable ones, and both happened in the band where nothing decays. The concern that follows is not that space will be full but that a chain of collisions could make particular altitudes unusable for generations, which is a slow process and not a dramatic one. Nothing about it would look like a disaster from the ground; it would look like an altitude that insurers stopped covering.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Avoiding a collision is a routine operation and an expensive one. Operators receive warnings of a possible close approach days in advance, with a probability attached, and decide whether to spend fuel on a manoeuvre; the fuel is the satellite’s lifetime, so a manoeuvre is a real cost. Most warnings turn out to be nothing, the uncertainty in the position of an untracked object is larger than the distances involved, and operators who manoeuvre for every warning would spend their missions dodging.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Disposal at the end of life is the cheapest remedy and is now written into licences. A satellite in a low orbit is required to be brought down within a set number of years, which is done by lowering its orbit with the last of its fuel; a satellite in a high orbit is instead pushed into a graveyard band above the useful ones. Compliance has improved and is not complete, and the objects that fail to comply are usually those that failed before the disposal could happen. A satellite that dies early takes its disposal plan with it, which is an argument for reserving the fuel rather than the intention.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Removing what is already there is harder than it sounds. A dead satellite tumbles, has no handles, may be leaking fuel and was never designed to be caught; proposals include nets, harpoons, robotic arms and a mission that attaches a motor and drags the object down. Several have been demonstrated on targets carried up for the purpose, which is not the same as catching something that has been tumbling for twenty years, and the cost per object removed is currently far above what anybody is willing to pay.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The economics are the difficulty rather than the engineering. Orbit is a commons: the cost of leaving an object there is paid by everybody who uses that altitude later, and the benefit of not spending fuel on disposal is kept by the operator. Proposals to fix this include deposits refunded on successful disposal, insurance priced by debris risk, and international rules with an enforcement mechanism that does not yet exist. The technical measures are agreed; the question of who pays is not.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What has changed the urgency is the number of satellites being launched. Constellations of thousands of small satellites in low orbit are now operating, with more planned, and their operators argue with some justification that their altitude clears itself within years. The counter-argument is about volume rather than about altitude: a larger number of objects means more close approaches, more manoeuvres, and more chances that a single failure happens where it matters. Nobody disputes the arithmetic; the disagreement is about what margin is prudent.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: The colour that built an industry

paragraphs.text: For most of history a bright colour was a luxury because it came from something rare. Red came from insects collected by hand, blue from a mineral mined in one region, purple from a shellfish in quantities that made a robe cost more than a house. Ordinary clothing was the colour of the fibre it was made from, and the word for a colour in many languages began as the name of the substance that produced it. Colour was a material before it was an idea, and it was priced accordingly.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The chemistry that changed this began with a mistake. A student working in a London laboratory in 1856 was trying to make a medicine from coal tar, failed, and noticed that the black residue in his flask dyed silk a strong purple that did not wash out. He was eighteen, he patented it within months, and he opened a factory with his father’s money against the advice of everybody who knew the dyeing trade. The advice was reasonable: nothing in the existing craft suggested that a coal-tar residue could be made in quantity or fixed to cloth reliably.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The colour arrived at exactly the right moment commercially. Purple had been the most expensive colour available and was therefore the most desired; a version that could be made by the tonne from a waste product of the gas industry sold as fast as it could be produced, and was worn by a queen within two years. The fashion passed, as fashions do, and by then the industry it started had moved on to other colours. Within fifteen years a dyer could order reds, greens and blues that no natural source had ever supplied in that strength.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: What followed was not a series of lucky accidents but a new way of working. Chemists learned to modify the structure of a molecule deliberately to change what it did, and dye became the first industry in which university chemistry and manufacturing were joined on purpose. Companies hired research staff, built laboratories beside their factories and patented compounds rather than processes, which is the pattern every science-based industry has followed since. The modern research laboratory is a nineteenth-century dye works with better ventilation.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The consequences reached medicine by an indirect route. A dye that stains one kind of cell and not another can reveal structures under a microscope, and the same selectivity suggested that a compound might attack a microbe and leave the patient alone. The first synthetic antibacterial drugs came out of dye laboratories, made by chemists who had spent their careers on colour, and the connection is the reason several large pharmaceutical companies began as dye works.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The colours also changed what could be recorded. Synthetic dyes gave photography its filters and film its emulsions, gave botanists and anatomists a way of showing what they had seen, and gave printing a reliable palette; a nineteenth-century illustration in colour is a chemical product as much as an artistic one. Textile designers who had worked within a narrow range found themselves choosing from hundreds of shades, and the visual character of the period changed within a generation. Paintings, posters and shop fronts from before and after the change are told apart by their colours before anything else.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The environmental record is poor and was known to be poor at the time. Dyeing uses very large quantities of water, and the effluent from the early works coloured rivers visibly enough that the pollution is documented in complaints rather than in measurements; several of the compounds used were later found to cause cancer in the people who made them. Modern regulation and treatment have changed this in the countries that enforce them, and the production has largely moved to countries where enforcement is weaker.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The industry today is unrecognisable in scale and familiar in structure. A handful of firms make most of the world’s dye, the chemistry is refined rather than new, and the pressures are environmental and regulatory rather than scientific. What survives from the beginning is the model: a laboratory attached to a factory, a patent on a molecule, and a market created by making something cheap that used to be reserved for the rich.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Is it worth restoring a building?

paragraphs.text: Every city has buildings that are too damaged to use and too loved to demolish, and the decision about what to do with them is made badly more often than it is made well. The choices are rarely as clean as the debate suggests: repair what stands, rebuild what has gone, replace the whole thing, or leave it as a ruin and stabilise it. Each answer suits some buildings and no answer suits all of them, and the argument usually proceeds as though one of them were a principle.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Johanna Brecht argues from the position that a building is its material. A wall rebuilt with new stone is a model of a wall, however accurate, and the information carried by the original — tool marks, repairs, the record of how it was actually built — is destroyed by the rebuilding rather than preserved by it. She accepts that this position is expensive and sometimes impractical, and insists that it be stated honestly when it is abandoned rather than disguised as restoration.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Samuel Aturu regards that as a museum view of a city. Buildings were altered by every generation that used them, he argues, and the version a conservation officer wants to freeze is simply the state it happened to be in when the rules were written; a building that cannot be changed becomes a building nobody can afford to keep, and the surest way to lose a structure is to make its owner unable to use it. His test is whether a change keeps the building in use for another fifty years.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Renata Alves works on what restoration does to a neighbourhood. A restored quarter attracts visitors and investment, and the people who lived there when it was cheap are frequently gone within a decade, so a project described as saving a place can preserve its buildings and replace its population. She does not treat this as an argument against restoration; she treats it as a cost that is never in the budget, and notes that the few schemes which planned for it, with protected rents and space reserved for existing trades, kept both.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Viktor Hase is interested in the carbon arithmetic, which has changed the argument in the past decade. Demolishing a masonry building and replacing it with a new one releases a great deal of carbon in the concrete and steel, and the new building has to run far more efficiently for a very long time to make that back; several analyses find that repair wins on this measure in most cases, including many where the existing structure is judged inefficient. He notes that this argument is now used by people who have no interest in heritage at all, which he regards as progress.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Reconstruction from nothing is the case where practice and principle diverge most sharply. Several cities rebuilt their historic centres after wars, in careful copies based on photographs and surveys, and the profession largely disapproved at the time; the rebuilt centres are now among the most valued places in those countries, and some carry international protection as reconstructions rather than as originals. Whatever the doctrine says, people who lose a place appear to want it back, and the buildings acquire an age of their own.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What the evidence supports is narrower than any of the positions. Repair is usually cheaper than replacement over a long horizon and usually better on carbon; a building kept in use survives better than one kept as an exhibit; reconstructions can become genuinely valued places; and none of this tells anybody what to do with a particular ruined church in a town that cannot pay for either option. The useful arguments are about this building, and the general ones consume the time that the particular ones need.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The practical test that several authorities now apply is closer to Aturu than to Brecht and stricter than either sounds. Before permission is given, the applicant has to show what will be lost and record it, show that the new use will pay for the maintenance, and show the carbon calculation for both options. It is a bureaucratic answer to an aesthetic argument, and it has the advantage of producing decisions that can be explained to somebody who disagrees with them.
paragraphs.label: H
